rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the scouting gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the tightly clustered middle and final peaks. All compounds currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent gradient shallowing.

Test the opposite temperature limit with the same gradient to distinguish temperature-sensitive selectivity from persistent co-elution. This completes a broad temperature screen before refining gradient slope and starting composition.

Retain the best temperature and make the gradient shallower to improve the two remaining critical pairs. The current last-peak time leaves substantial room to gain resolution without incurring a time penalty.

The middle critical pair worsened as the gradient became shallower, suggesting an approaching or completed elution-order crossover. Test further shallowing to separate it on the other side, while raising the starting organic fraction to keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient with a modest temperature increase to move the middle critical pair away from its selectivity crossover. The elevated starting composition should help contain retention time while preserving separation of the later pair.

Increase the gradient slope at 30 C to bring the last peak below 10 minutes and test whether the two new critical pairs move away from co-elution. Keeping starting composition and temperature fixed isolates the slope response.

Return to 25 C and further shallow the gradient from injection 5 to test separation beyond the middle-pair crossover. The higher starting organic fraction should keep the final peak near or below 10 minutes while improving late-pair resolution.

Injection 8 achieved the maximum CRF; now raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten elution while retaining a shallow gradient. Check whether the critical middle pair remains fully resolved, keeping injection 8 as the validated fallback.

Restore the starting composition of the fully resolved method and shorten its gradient by one grid step. This tests the speed–resolution boundary directly; injection 8 remains the maximum-score fallback if the middle pair drops below R = 1.5.

Shortening the gradient lost full resolution, so restore 28 minutes and test a one-step temperature increase instead. This may shorten retention while preserving separation, with injection 8 retained as the proven maximum-CRF method.

At 30 C, a slightly steeper gradient may improve the final pair, as seen in the earlier slope comparison, while shortening the run. Check whether the two middle pairs retain full resolution; injection 8 remains the maximum-score fallback.

The middle pair approached co-elution when the starting fraction rose from 0.25 to 0.30; another step may separate it on the opposite side of that crossover. Test this faster elution window while retaining injection 8 as the proven maximum-score method.

Injection 13 retained maximum CRF with much faster elution, so raise the starting organic fraction one more step. Monitor the middle cluster and early peaks for loss of resolution as retention decreases.

Back off to the fully resolved starting composition and shorten the gradient to accelerate the late peaks. This tests whether injection 13's resolution margins permit a substantially faster method without sacrificing maximum CRF.

Shorten the gradient further at the successful starting composition and temperature. The late critical pair is likely to approach its resolution limit, so this run will bracket the fastest fully resolved gradient.
Back off one gradient-duration step from the under-resolved 10-minute method. This should improve both deficient pairs while retaining most of the speed gain over injection 15.

Test a one-step temperature increase on the fastest fully resolved method to seek shorter retention. Monitor the middle cluster for selectivity changes, retaining injection 17 as the maximum-CRF fallback.

The middle pair converged between 25 and 30 C; test a larger temperature shift for separation beyond that crossover and faster elution. Injection 17 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method if other pairs become critical.

Return to the favorable 25 C temperature and test a higher-organic window beyond the middle-pair crossover suggested by injection 14. This explores faster separation on the opposite side of that crossover, with early-peak resolution also checked carefully.

Test whether higher starting organic and temperature separate the middle pair beyond its crossover in a faster elution window. This is an exploratory speed improvement; injection 17 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Steepen the gradient at the promising fast conditions of injection 21 to test whether the remaining middle pair separates further beyond its crossover. Monitor the neighboring pairs, which have limited resolution margin, while retaining injection 17 as the validated fallback.

The remaining middle pair barely responded to slope, so test a temperature-driven selectivity change instead. Use a somewhat shallower gradient to protect neighboring pairs while seeking a fully resolved method faster than injection 17.

Refine around injection 17 by testing a slope halfway between its fully resolved gradient and injection 16's faster, under-resolved gradient. Lowering the endpoint to 0.90 permits this intermediate slope on the instrument grid and may shorten elution while preserving maximum CRF.

Match injection 17's fully resolved slope while narrowing the gradient window and shortening its programmed duration. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the validated last peak at 4.14 minutes, so the separation should retain maximum CRF.
